courses.title: 1. Bits, binary and buses
courses.summary: Represent information with switches, read binary numbers and define the signal contracts that let independently built modules connect.

lessons.title: A bit is an agreement
paragraphs: A bit has two allowed logical values, 0 and 1. A lamp, voltage range, lever position or mark on paper can represent them. The physical object is not the information: the agreement about how to interpret its state is. Decide which condition means 1 before connecting two modules.

Digital abstraction deliberately ignores some physical detail. A redstone line has strength and delay; an electronic wire has a voltage and noise. A useful gate must restore a valid output and produce the promised answer after inputs settle. This bench computes ideal values, so a correct result here is a functional specification for a physical build.
lessons.example:
lever off → 0
lever on  → 1
lessons.pitfall: Treating an intermediate or unreliable signal as a dependable third Boolean value.

question.prompt: What must two modules agree on before sharing a signal?

options.text: The programming language used to describe them

question.explanation: A shared encoding lets one module interpret another module’s output.

lessons.title: Position gives a bit its weight
paragraphs: Read a four-bit bus as B3 B2 B1 B0, with B0 the least significant bit. Its unsigned value is 8B3 + 4B2 + 2B1 + B0. There are sixteen patterns, numbered 0 through 15. The leftmost displayed bit is not automatically the first physical wire; label the wires.

For 0101, the 4 and 1 places are set, giving five. Moving the same bit from position 0 to position 3 changes its weight from one to eight. The lab lists input buttons in increasing index order, so write the conventional most-significant-first representation separately when interpreting the bus.
lessons.pitfall: Reading B0 B1 B2 B3 as if B0 had the weight eight.

question.prompt: What unsigned value does B3 B2 B1 B0 = 1010 represent?
question.explanation: The set places have weights eight and two.

lessons.title: Numbers are interpretations
paragraphs: A bus does not inherently know whether its bits mean a number, character, address or instruction. Hexadecimal is compact notation: each hex digit names four bits. Decimal 10, binary 1010 and hexadecimal A can describe the same four physical bits.

Signed two’s-complement is another interpretation. Four-bit 1111 can mean unsigned 15 or signed −1. The arithmetic circuit can keep the same bits while software chooses how to interpret them. Our VQ4 CPU uses modulo-16 arithmetic; it does not store a separate minus sign.
lessons.example:
hex 0…F ↔ binary 0000…1111
1111: unsigned 15; signed −1
lessons.pitfall: Assuming an instruction and a number require physically different kinds of bits.

question.prompt: Does 1111 always mean fifteen?

options.text: No; it always means negative one
No; the chosen encoding determines its meaning
Yes; bits have only one meaning

question.explanation: An unsigned and a signed interpretation assign different values to the same pattern.

lessons.title: A bus is several named signals
paragraphs: A four-bit parallel bus has four distinct bit signals. It is not a single redstone dust line with sixteen possible strengths. You can design an analog-strength encoding too, but then you need different interfaces and decoding. In this path each wire carries one Boolean bit.

Write a module contract with input names, widths, bit order, valid output behavior and when the output is stable. Keep data, address and control signals distinguishable. A block layout can change radically while that contract stays the same; this is what makes the design transferable to gates, relays or Minecraft.
lessons.example: Contract: input B[3:0], output Y[3:0]; Y = B after settling.
lessons.pitfall: Connecting buses by appearance without checking bit order and width.

question.prompt: How many one-bit lines carry an ordinary parallel four-bit bus?
question.explanation: Each line carries one of the four bit positions.

steps: Start with B2 and B0 on. Read the outputs as 0101, or five.
Turn only B3 on and turn the other bits off; predict eight before checking.
Generate the truth table and find all sixteen input patterns.
Draw four labelled wires in your chosen medium and record which end is bit zero.

bridge.other: Use four switches and indicators, or paper tokens. Signal voltage, material and geometry belong to the implementation, not the binary equation.

acceptance: List all sixteen patterns and their unsigned values.
Include bit order, the meaning of on/off and a single-bit wiring test.

questions.prompt: How many patterns can three bits encode?
questions.explanation: Each additional bit doubles the number of patterns.

questions.prompt: What is 1100₂ as unsigned decimal?
questions.explanation: Eight plus four is twelve.

questions.prompt: Which notation names the same four-bit value as decimal 15?
questions.explanation: Hex F represents fifteen; hex 10 needs five binary bits.

questions.prompt: What should be checked when a displayed value is bit-reversed?

options.text: The language of the assembly comments

questions.explanation: Swapping the significance of wires reverses the encoding.

questions.prompt: What survives when switches are replaced with redstone levers?
questions.explanation: The abstract function can remain the same while its physical implementation changes.

courses.title: 2. Logic gates and truth tables
courses.summary: Learn NOT, AND, OR, XOR, NAND, NOR and XNOR by predicting every input combination.

lessons.title: Inversion and conjunction
paragraphs: NOT reverses one bit. AND produces 1 only when both inputs are 1. These are rules about values, not particular shapes: the same rule can be implemented with transistors, relays or redstone. A useful first exercise is to describe the rule in plain language before drawing a circuit.

An enabled door could use AND of permission and a request. If the request is active-low, invert it before applying the rule. Naming the polarity matters as much as choosing the gate; an unlabeled inverted input can make a seemingly correct circuit do the opposite of the requirement.
lessons.pitfall: Assuming a gate follows its name without checking whether an input is active-low.

question.prompt: When does a two-input AND produce 1?
question.explanation: AND requires both conditions.

lessons.title: Inclusive OR and exclusive OR
paragraphs: OR is inclusive: either input or both can make its output 1. XOR is exclusive for two inputs: it reports whether they differ. With both inputs on, OR is 1 and XOR is 0. That one row distinguishes two gates that can look similar in casual language.

XOR will become the low bit of addition because one plus zero gives one, but one plus one gives a low bit zero and a separate carry. Chaining XOR across more inputs computes parity, not the rule “exactly one input is on.” Three on bits have odd parity and therefore produce 1.
lessons.pitfall: Calling a multi-input XOR an exactly-one detector.

question.prompt: For A=1 and B=1, what are OR and XOR?
question.explanation: Inclusive OR allows both; two-input XOR requires different inputs.

lessons.title: Negated outputs and equality
paragraphs: NAND is NOT of AND, NOR is NOT of OR, and XNOR is NOT of XOR. The N indicates output inversion, not that every input is independently inverted. XNOR is a one-bit equality check: it produces 1 for both 00 and 11.

To compare two four-bit words, XNOR corresponding bits and AND the four equality results. OR-ing them would merely say at least one bit matches. Build the word operation from the bit contract; this compositional reasoning scales beyond a single gate.
lessons.example:
XNOR(A,B) = NOT XOR(A,B)
word_equal = eq0 AND eq1 AND eq2 AND eq3
lessons.pitfall: Using OR to combine equality tests when all bit positions must match.

question.prompt: Which two-input gate reports equal bits?
question.explanation: XNOR is 1 for 00 and 11.

lessons.title: Exhaustive tests beat a convincing example
paragraphs: Two independent bit inputs have four combinations. A complete truth table checks all four, including 00 and 11. Testing only 01 can make OR and XOR appear identical. Predict the output, apply the inputs, wait for settling in a physical build, and compare the observation with the prediction.

When a module fails, first test its inputs and output separately. Distinguish a wrong Boolean equation from wrong physical placement. A circuit that works only with a favorable update order is not a reliable implementation of its static truth table. The lab table evaluates the actual edited network.
lessons.example: Test order: 00 → 01 → 10 → 11
lessons.pitfall: Treating one successful lever combination as proof of a gate.

question.prompt: How many rows fully test two independent bit inputs?
question.explanation: There are 2² possible input assignments.

steps: Predict all seven outputs for A=1, B=0 before inspecting them.
Set both inputs to 1; compare OR with XOR and NAND with NOR.
Generate the truth table and explain the 00 row.
Edit one gate type, evaluate the circuit again and see which table entries change.
courses.expected: The starting outputs are NOT=0, AND=0, OR=1, XOR=1, NAND=1, NOR=0 and XNOR=0.

bridge.principle: A truth table is a portable test specification for a gate.
bridge.minecraft: Build isolated two-input modules, using levers for A/B and a lamp for the result. Test all four rows in the edition you use; record the orientation and settling time.
bridge.other: Implement the same tables with electronic logic ICs or relay contacts, respecting their own power and signal requirements.

challenge.task: Make a gate test sheet that distinguishes OR, XOR and XNOR.
acceptance: Include both equal-input rows and both different-input rows.
Record predicted and observed values separately.

questions.prompt: What is NOR(0,0)?
questions.explanation: NOR inverts OR, which is zero for two zero inputs.

questions.prompt: What is NAND(1,1)?
questions.explanation: The AND result is one, then inversion makes it zero.

questions.prompt: Three 1 bits are XORed in sequence. What is the result?
questions.explanation: 1 XOR 1 is 0, then 0 XOR 1 is 1: odd parity.

questions.prompt: Which input row distinguishes OR from XOR?
questions.explanation: OR includes the both-true case; XOR excludes it.

questions.prompt: To test a gate in another medium, what should remain identical?

options.text: Expected results for every valid input row

questions.explanation: The behavior is portable; timing and geometry need separate verification.

courses.title: 3. Build gates from NAND
courses.summary: Discover functional completeness and compose a working XOR using only four NAND gates.

lessons.title: One gate family can be enough
paragraphs: A functionally complete gate family can express every Boolean combinational function. NAND alone is sufficient because it can construct NOT, AND and OR, which can implement any finite truth table. This is a statement about logical expressiveness, not a promise of minimum area or fastest operation.

Tie both NAND inputs to A. AND of A with itself is A, so the inverted output is NOT A. Feeding one output to multiple gate inputs is fan-out. The ideal model allows it freely; a physical implementation must still deliver a valid signal to every load.
lessons.example: NOT A = NAND(A,A)
lessons.pitfall: Assuming functional completeness also gives memory without feedback or clocked storage.

question.prompt: How do you make NOT using one NAND?

options.text: Connect the output directly to itself

question.explanation: NAND(A,A) is the complement of A.

lessons.title: AND and OR through inversion
paragraphs: Build AND by inverting the output of NAND. For OR, use De Morgan’s identity: A OR B = NOT(NOT A AND NOT B). Two input inverters and a final NAND implement that identity. Trace intermediate values rather than trusting a memorized block picture.

At A=0, B=1, the inverted inputs are 1 and 0; their NAND is 1, as OR requires. Replacing one of the NANDs with an AND changes the function. The connection pattern is part of the proof. Keep intermediate nets named so another learner can follow it.
lessons.example:
n = NAND A B
y = NAND n n
; y = A AND B
lessons.pitfall: Inverting the output when the identity requires inverted inputs instead.

question.prompt: Which identity implements OR with NAND and input inversion?

options.text: A OR B = AND(NOT A, NOT B)
A OR B = NAND(NOT A, NOT B)

question.explanation: De Morgan’s law moves the inversion across the AND and complements both inputs.

lessons.title: Four NANDs make XOR
paragraphs: Let p=NAND(A,B), q=NAND(A,p), r=NAND(B,p), and X=NAND(q,r). When exactly one input is 1, q and r differ and X becomes 1. When both are 0 or both are 1, q and r are both 1 and X is 0.

This is a concrete example of abstraction: after verifying its four rows, draw a box around the network and label it XOR. A full adder can use the box without knowing which physical blocks implement it. If you change its internals, rerun the same external tests.
lessons.example:
p=NAND(A,B); q=NAND(A,p)
r=NAND(B,p); X=NAND(q,r)
lessons.pitfall: Assuming the internal net p is itself the final XOR result.

question.prompt: For A=B=1, what are p and X in this network?
question.explanation: p becomes zero; q and r become one; their NAND is zero.

lessons.title: Cost is more than gate count
paragraphs: The NAND XOR uses four gates, but its longest input-to-output path passes through three. Logic depth is one clue about delay. The bench counts each combinational gate as one abstract stage; real gates and redstone components have unequal delays and different drive behavior.

Reusing an intermediate signal can reduce gate count while increasing fan-out. A compact redstone arrangement may introduce unwanted coupling. Optimize after proving behavior, and measure timing in the actual build. A minimum logical formula is not necessarily the easiest structure to route.
lessons.example: NAND XOR: 4 gates; longest dependency path = 3 stages
lessons.pitfall: Calling a three-stage logical path exactly three Minecraft ticks.

question.prompt: What does the bench’s logic depth measure?

options.text: The longest chain of combinational gate dependencies
The number of bits in the output

question.explanation: It is a structural count, not a timing simulation.

steps: Evaluate the NAND-only preset for both inputs on; expect X=0.
Generate all four rows and compare with XOR from the preceding course.
Change r to NAND A p and find a counterexample in the table.
Restore the source and identify the longest dependency path from an input to X.
courses.expected: The original network has four NAND gates, depth three, and output sequence 0,1,1,0 for 00,01,10,11.

bridge.principle: Verify a module once, then reuse its external contract at the next level.
bridge.minecraft: Build and label one NAND module first. Four verified copies can implement the XOR network; ensure output connections cannot feed power backwards into neighboring modules.
bridge.other: Swap NAND blocks for transistor or relay implementations without changing the network’s truth table.

challenge.task: Implement AND and OR using only NAND, then compare them with the built-in gates.
acceptance: Supply complete truth tables.
Count gates and dependency depth separately.

questions.prompt: How many NAND gates are sufficient for the given XOR network?
questions.explanation: The authored p,q,r,X construction uses four NANDs.

questions.prompt: What is NAND(NAND(A,B), NAND(A,B))?
questions.explanation: The outer NAND inverts the inner result.

questions.prompt: Does NAND completeness mean all circuits have equal speed?

options.text: No; implementation depth and physical delays differ
Yes; every gate has the same function
Yes; all circuits contain one NAND

questions.explanation: Completeness concerns which functions can be represented.

questions.prompt: What should be tested after replacing XOR internals?
questions.explanation: The replacement must preserve the full contract.

questions.prompt: Why name intermediate nets?

options.text: To trace values and diagnose the first wrong stage

questions.explanation: Names expose the composition and help locate faults.

courses.title: 4. Boolean design from a requirement
courses.summary: Turn a majority-vote requirement into a truth table, derive a circuit and verify simplifications.

lessons.title: Start with the required behavior
paragraphs: Suppose three sensors vote A, B and C, and a result should be 1 when at least two vote yes. Write all eight rows before choosing gates. Rows 011,101,110 and 111 should produce 1. A phrase such as “two sensors” needs this precision: exactly two and at least two disagree on 111.

Requirements are easier to discuss as input/output examples than as a block arrangement. Include boundary rows, state the input polarity and decide whether the function remembers anything. Majority voting here is purely combinational and has no previous-state input.
lessons.pitfall: Building before resolving “exactly two” versus “at least two.”

question.prompt: Should majority voting output 1 for 111?

options.text: Yes, at least two inputs are on
No, only exactly two are allowed

question.explanation: This requirement is combinational and includes three yes votes.

lessons.title: Sum of products
paragraphs: Each true row can be expressed as an AND term of input bits or their complements. OR the terms to cover all true rows. This systematic construction works for any finite truth table, although the result can be large. Here, pairs already cover the desired rows: AB, AC and BC.

The majority expression is (A AND B) OR (A AND C) OR (B AND C). A true pair guarantees at least two votes; any row with two votes contains at least one true pair. That two-direction argument explains why the expression matches the requirement.
lessons.example:
Y = AB + AC + BC
Here adjacency means AND and + means OR, not numeric addition.
lessons.pitfall: Reading Boolean + as arithmetic addition and expecting outputs above one.

question.prompt: Which expression implements three-input majority?
question.explanation: Every accepted input has a true pair; every true pair satisfies the requirement.

lessons.title: Simplify while preserving meaning
paragraphs: A factored form is AB OR C(A OR B). Factoring shares logic and may alter routing or depth, but the truth table must stay unchanged. Boolean identities such as A OR A = A and A AND 1 = A help simplify; they are not ordinary arithmetic rules.

Keep an unoptimized reference specification and compare every possible row of a small circuit. For large circuits, use directed cases plus a stronger verification method where needed. A shorter expression is a proposed optimization until its equivalence is demonstrated.
lessons.example: AB + AC + BC = AB + C(A + B)
lessons.pitfall: Removing a term because its first test case also happens to satisfy another term.

question.prompt: How can you prove these two three-input circuits equivalent in this bench?
question.explanation: Matching every possible input establishes Boolean equivalence.

lessons.title: Functional correctness and hazards
paragraphs: Even equivalent formulas may behave differently while inputs are changing. Unequal delays can create a brief glitch before the final output settles. The ideal bench reports final Boolean values and abstract depth; it does not simulate those transient hazards.

When a combinational output controls a stored value, provide time for the slowest path to settle before sampling. In a redstone build, test transitions as well as static lever settings and slow the clock during diagnosis. Do not use a glitched combinational line as a clock without a designed timing strategy.
lessons.example:
Static test: every input row
Dynamic test: input transition → wait → sample
lessons.pitfall: Concluding that a truth-table pass proves glitch-free physical behavior.

question.prompt: What does a correct static truth table leave unproven?

options.text: The settled result for a tested row

question.explanation: Static equivalence does not model unequal propagation delays.

steps: Generate the eight-row table; locate exactly four rows with Y=1.
Set A=1,B=0,C=1; verify Y=1, then remove C and verify Y=0.
Replace the network with AB OR C(A OR B) and compare every row.
Write a transition test for a physical build and decide when it is safe to sample.
courses.expected: The majority output is 1 for 011,101,110,111 and 0 for the other four rows.

bridge.principle: Specify, derive, test and only then optimize the physical arrangement.
bridge.minecraft: Use three levers and a result lamp for a voting module. Space paths to avoid accidental joins; test input transitions after the eight static cases.
bridge.other: The same majority module can vote on redundant digital sensors or choose a game rule, though actual fault tolerance requires additional system design.

challenge.task: Create an exactly-two voter, then explain its difference from majority.
acceptance: Its 111 output must be 0.
Document the full table and a gate implementation.

questions.prompt: How many combinations do three Boolean inputs have?
questions.explanation: Each independent input doubles the combinations.

questions.prompt: Which majority input should produce zero?
questions.explanation: Only one yes vote is present.

questions.prompt: What does A OR A simplify to?
questions.explanation: Duplicating the same condition does not add a new true case.

questions.prompt: If two expressions match all eight rows, what is established?
questions.explanation: All possible stable input values produce matching outputs.

questions.prompt: Why wait before storing the result of a physical gate network?

options.text: Because binary values require decimal conversion
Different paths need time to settle

questions.explanation: Propagation delays can temporarily expose intermediate values.

courses.title: 5. Half adders and full adders
courses.summary: Build addition from XOR, AND and OR, with a separate sum bit and carry bit.

lessons.title: Two outputs represent a two-bit result
paragraphs: Adding two one-bit inputs has possible totals 0,1 and 2. One output bit cannot encode all three values. A half adder produces S=A XOR B and C=A AND B, where the numeric total equals 2C+S. For 1+1, S=0 and C=1.

The carry is not an error. It is the high part of the result. Label the two outputs separately so a consumer does not confuse the sum with the full numeric answer. This is the first step from Boolean decisions to arithmetic hardware.
lessons.pitfall: Expecting the sum bit alone to contain the number two.

question.prompt: What does a half adder output for 1+1?
question.explanation: The result two is binary 10.

lessons.title: Include an incoming carry
paragraphs: A full adder accepts A, B and CIN. First compute P=A XOR B. Then S=P XOR CIN. A carry occurs if A and B are both 1, or if P and CIN are both 1. Thus COUT=(A AND B) OR (P AND CIN).

This can be understood as two half adders plus an OR. The incoming carry is the contribution from the less significant column. For three ones the total is three, represented by COUT=1 and S=1. It still needs only two output bits.
lessons.example:
S = A XOR B XOR CIN
COUT = AB OR ((A XOR B) AND CIN)
lessons.pitfall: Dropping CIN when moving beyond the least significant column.

question.prompt: What is the full-adder result for A=B=CIN=1?
question.explanation: The total three is binary 11.

lessons.title: Test the arithmetic invariant
paragraphs: There are eight input triples. For each one, compute the ordinary integer sum A+B+CIN, then check it equals S+2COUT. This is an independent specification: the test does not repeat the gate expression you are trying to verify.

Pairs with one or two set inputs are useful because they exercise both ways of creating carry. The lab shows intermediate propagate and generate nets. If a result is wrong, follow the first mismatch from the inputs rather than changing random connections.
lessons.example: A + B + CIN = S + 2×COUT for every input triple
lessons.pitfall: Testing the carry with only the 111 case.

question.prompt: Which equation verifies a full adder independently?
question.explanation: Weight two belongs to the carry output.

lessons.title: Make a reusable one-bit slice
paragraphs: Once the full adder is verified, give it a stable interface: A, B, CIN, S and COUT. Place identical copies in bit order, with carry moving from the least significant slice to the next. The physical layout should make the carry direction obvious.

You may choose a NAND-only implementation internally and keep the interface. In a physical build record the delay from each input to S and COUT; the carry path can be the limiting path when many slices are joined. A working slice is valuable because it can be tested before replication.
lessons.example: slice0.COUT → slice1.CIN
lessons.pitfall: Copying an unverified slice many times and multiplying the same fault.

question.prompt: Which connection joins consecutive addition columns?

options.text: Lower slice COUT to higher slice CIN

question.explanation: Carry contributes to the next more significant column.

steps: With A=B=CIN=1, verify S=1 and COUT=1.
Generate the eight rows and calculate S+2COUT for each.
Set only CIN=1 to show why the carry input cannot be omitted.
Trace the intermediate p, g and h signals, then draw one reusable slice.
courses.expected: For the starting triple 111, S=1 and COUT=1. Every table row satisfies A+B+CIN=S+2COUT.

bridge.principle: A reusable arithmetic slice depends on a tested interface, not a particular gate layout.
bridge.minecraft: Place the carry input and output on opposite ends of a redstone full-adder module. Prove all eight cases before making four copies.
bridge.other: Chain identical slices using any technology that implements XOR, AND and OR with compatible signals.

challenge.task: Build a full adder using only NAND gates.
acceptance: Test all eight triples against the arithmetic invariant.
Record the carry direction and the longest dependency path.

questions.prompt: What is the half-adder sum equation?
questions.explanation: XOR matches the low bit of the sum.

questions.prompt: What is the result of 1+0+1?
questions.explanation: The total is two.

questions.prompt: How many cases fully test a full adder?
questions.explanation: A, B and CIN are three independent bits.

questions.prompt: What weight does COUT have relative to S?
questions.explanation: It belongs to the next binary position.

questions.prompt: Why test a slice before copying it?

options.text: To make the sum use decimal encoding
A repeated wiring error would affect every column
To remove the need for clock timing

questions.explanation: Local verification helps isolate faults before composition.

courses.title: 6. Ripple carry, subtraction and overflow
courses.summary: Scale the full adder to four bits and distinguish carry, signed overflow and modulo arithmetic.

lessons.title: Carry ripples toward higher bits
paragraphs: Join four full adders so bit zero receives CIN and each higher slice receives the preceding carry. Each slice computes only its own sum bit. The final carry is a fifth output, while S3…S0 form the four-bit result.

For 7+1, carry passes through three low columns before setting the high bit. If you connect the slices in reverse, the bit weights no longer match addition. In a physical circuit the output is valid only after the relevant carry propagation completes.
lessons.pitfall: Treating every slice’s carry input as the external CIN.

question.prompt: In a four-bit ripple adder, where does bit two get carry?
question.explanation: Carry travels toward increasing bit significance.

lessons.title: A fixed-width result wraps
paragraphs: Four output bits can retain only the result modulo sixteen. Adding fifteen and one produces S=0000 and COUT=1. The identity A+B+CIN=S+16COUT connects the retained result with the full unsigned sum.

Discarding carry is sometimes intentional, as in a wrapping counter. Sometimes carry triggers a wider operation. The arithmetic circuit should expose it even if a particular instruction ignores it. Avoid calling every wraparound a bug; compare it with the selected numeric contract.
lessons.pitfall: Assuming a four-bit output can display sixteen without another bit.

question.prompt: What are S and COUT for 15+1 with CIN=0?
question.explanation: Sixteen needs five bits; the low four wrap to zero.

lessons.title: Subtraction reuses addition
paragraphs: For a four-bit result, A−B can be computed as A + NOT(B) + 1. Complement all four B bits and set CIN=1. The result is taken modulo sixteen. This is the hardware reason two’s-complement arithmetic is convenient.

Under this construction a final carry of 1 means no unsigned borrow was needed. For 3−5, use 3+10+1=14, giving 1110 and carry 0. As a signed four-bit value, 1110 is −2. CPU families differ in how they name and encode subtraction flags; this course’s VQ4 uses C=1 for no borrow.
lessons.pitfall: Assuming every processor uses the same borrow-flag convention.

question.prompt: To subtract B using the adder, what do you change?

options.text: Set CIN=0 and leave B unchanged

question.explanation: A + complement(B) + 1 computes two’s-complement subtraction.

lessons.title: Carry is not signed overflow
paragraphs: Unsigned four-bit values range from 0 to 15; signed two’s-complement values range from −8 to 7. The same 0111+0001 circuit result is 1000 with no final carry. As signed arithmetic, 7+1 has overflowed the representable positive range.

For addition, signed overflow occurs when equal-sign operands produce an opposite-sign result. VQ4 exposes Z and C, not a separate signed-overflow flag. Its programs must choose an interpretation and avoid claiming that C alone proves signed correctness.
lessons.example:
7 + 1: C=0, signed overflow=yes
15 + 1: C=1, unsigned wrap=yes
lessons.pitfall: Using carry as the signed-overflow flag.

question.prompt: Does C=0 prove that signed addition did not overflow?

options.text: Only when the result is displayed in hex

question.explanation: Signed range and unsigned carry are different properties.

steps: Evaluate the initial 7+1 preset; read S3…S0 as 1000.
Turn A3 on to make A=15, keeping B=1; expect zero with COUT=1.
For 3−5 set A=0011, B=1010 and CIN=1; expect S=1110 and COUT=0.
Inspect the carry nodes f0c through f3c and explain the direction of propagation.
courses.expected: The initial sum is eight with carry zero. Changing A to fifteen produces zero with carry one.

bridge.principle: Word width and interpretation determine what arithmetic results mean.
bridge.minecraft: Build four verified slices and leave a visible carry lamp. Start with a manual clock or static inputs; size the wait time for the longest path rather than one torch.
bridge.other: Use the same adder in a counter, ALU or wider ripple chain after checking fan-out and settling in the chosen hardware.

challenge.task: Design a four-bit add/subtract module with a SUB control.
acceptance: Use XOR with SUB on each B bit and connect SUB to CIN.
Test 0−1, 15+1, equal operands and 7+1 under signed and unsigned interpretations.

questions.explanation: Sixteen patterns encode sixteen values starting at zero.

questions.prompt: What does four-bit 0−1 produce?
questions.explanation: Modulo-sixteen subtraction wraps to fifteen.

questions.prompt: What is the signed range of four-bit two’s complement?
questions.explanation: The sign bit has weight minus eight.

questions.prompt: For four-bit 7+1, which statement is true?

options.text: Signed overflow occurs without final carry

questions.explanation: 1000 is outside the positive signed range despite C=0.

questions.prompt: In the documented VQ4 subtraction convention, C=1 means what?
questions.explanation: VQ4 keeps the carry from A+NOT(B)+1.

courses.title: 7. Multiplexers, decoders and buses
courses.summary: Select data and destinations with gates, then use those patterns to connect a CPU’s datapath.

lessons.title: A multiplexer chooses one value
paragraphs: A two-to-one multiplexer has data inputs D0/D1 and a select bit S. When S=0 it returns D0; when S=1 it returns D1. One equation is (NOT S AND D0) OR (S AND D1). The select is control information, while D0 and D1 are data.

A four-bit mux repeats this one-bit rule four times with the same select. That lets an accumulator choose between memory and an arithmetic result. In the circuit language, MUX D0 D1 S lists the selector last; its position matters.
lessons.example:
Y = MUX D0 D1 S
S=0 → D0; S=1 → D1
lessons.pitfall: Treating MUX as a three-input OR gate.

question.prompt: What does MUX D0 D1 1 select?
question.explanation: The third input selects the second data input when it is one.

lessons.title: Decode an address
paragraphs: A two-to-four decoder turns address A1 A0 into one of four active lines. The terms are NOT A1 AND NOT A0, NOT A1 AND A0, A1 AND NOT A0, and A1 AND A0. Exactly one term is true for a stable valid binary address.

Memory write selection combines each decoded line with a write-enable signal. Address 10 selects word two, not two words at once. With a real decoder, input transitions may briefly glitch; avoid writing while address signals are changing.
lessons.pitfall: Confusing an address’s numeric value with the count of enabled outputs.

question.prompt: Which line should address A1 A0=10 select?
question.explanation: Binary 10 is address two.

lessons.title: One source at a time
paragraphs: A shared data path needs a rule selecting which source drives it. A mux makes the choice explicit. Physically tying outputs together is a different circuit: a wired-OR implementation may combine them, and incompatible electrical drivers can conflict. Neither automatically means “choose the right value.”

The VQ4 teaching datapath uses selection logic rather than electrical tri-state simulation. To transfer the design, identify every bus source and its enable. Check exclusivity, inactive behavior and what happens during transitions before attaching storage inputs.
lessons.example: destination = select ? source1 : source0
lessons.pitfall: Joining redstone lines and calling the result a multiplexer.

question.prompt: Why is simply joining two output wires not generally a mux?

options.text: It does not implement exclusive selection
It always produces the larger binary word

question.explanation: A mux needs a control rule that chooses one source.

lessons.title: Demultiplexing and scalable selection
paragraphs: A demultiplexer routes one input to one of several destinations: each output is data AND its decoded select. A decoder itself has no arbitrary data input. These related ideas appear in write enables, instruction decoding and display selection.

Larger selectors can be built as trees. A four-to-one mux uses two first-level muxes and one final mux. Verify both data behavior and select-bit order. If one address accesses the wrong word, check the mapping of high and low address bits before blaming storage.
lessons.example: Y0 = D AND W0; Y1 = D AND W1; …
lessons.pitfall: Assuming decoder outputs themselves contain the selected data word.

question.prompt: What is needed to turn a decoder into a data demultiplexer?

options.text: AND each select output with the data input
Add a clock to every output

question.explanation: The decoder chooses the destination and the AND gates gate the data.

steps: At the preset A1=0,A0=1, verify only W1 is on and Y equals D1.
Step through all four addresses and check one-hot decoder outputs.
Change D0 and D1 independently while keeping A0 fixed; the unselected source must not affect Y.
Generate all sixteen combinations to test decoder and selector together.
courses.expected: Initially W1=1, the other decoded lines are zero, and Y=1 from D1.

bridge.principle: Data paths need explicit selection; addresses need a documented mapping to enables.
bridge.minecraft: Keep address lines separate from data. Build a one-hot row selector, then gate writes with a separate enable; never allow a changing address to write multiple memory rows.
bridge.other: Multiplexer and decoder contracts also apply to FPGA logic, relay routing and electronic register files.

challenge.task: Build a four-input one-bit multiplexer from three MUX nodes.
acceptance: Test each address with only its selected data bit on.
Show that toggling an unselected bit leaves Y unchanged.

questions.prompt: What does a mux do?

options.text: Select one of several data values

questions.explanation: A multiplexer chooses a source under control of select inputs.

questions.prompt: How many addresses do two bits select?
questions.explanation: Two bits encode four choices.

questions.prompt: For a stable two-to-four decoder, how many lines are active?
questions.explanation: The decoded outputs represent mutually exclusive addresses.

questions.prompt: Which signal should gate a memory write in addition to the address?
questions.explanation: Addressing alone should not cause data to be stored.

questions.prompt: Which select input is last in MUX D0 D1 S?
questions.explanation: The language explicitly separates two data inputs from a final selector.

courses.title: 8. Build a four-bit ALU
courses.summary: Combine arithmetic, bitwise logic, selectors and status outputs into the core of a processor.

lessons.title: Many functions, one selected result
paragraphs: An arithmetic-logic unit takes operands and a control value describing the requested operation. Our gate-level lab computes AND, OR, XOR and ADD in parallel, then uses muxes to select one result. The operation code OP1 OP0 is 00,01,10 or 11 respectively.

The function blocks are not intelligent: they always obey their gate equations. The control unit supplies selection bits. Distinguishing those roles makes a CPU easier to build because the ALU can be tested long before instruction decoding exists.
lessons.example: OP1 OP0: 00 AND, 01 OR, 10 XOR, 11 ADD
lessons.pitfall: Assuming an ALU decides which instruction to execute.

question.prompt: Who selects the ALU operation in a CPU?
question.explanation: Instruction decoding produces the control signals.

lessons.title: Bitwise logic differs from arithmetic
paragraphs: With A=0011 and B=0101, AND gives 0001, OR gives 0111 and XOR gives 0110. These operations treat corresponding bits independently. Addition gives 1000 because carries connect the bit positions.

A bit mask can clear unwanted bits with AND, set selected bits with OR, or toggle bits with XOR. These operations are useful for controlling indicator panels and extracting instruction fields. They do not require interpreting the bus as a signed number.
lessons.pitfall: Confusing bitwise AND with a single true/false test of whole numbers.

question.prompt: What is 0011 XOR 0101?
question.explanation: XOR sets exactly the positions that differ.

lessons.title: Status outputs summarize the selected result
paragraphs: The zero flag Z is 1 exactly when every selected result bit is zero. OR all four result bits and invert the result. Carry C belongs to addition in this lab, so it is gated off for the three logical operations.

Flags must describe the selected result, not an unrelated parallel function. A CPU stores flags at a defined instruction boundary. The combinational ALU lab displays them immediately after settling, while later CPU lessons add state and define which instructions update them.
lessons.example:
Z = NOT(Y0 OR Y1 OR Y2 OR Y3)
C = addition_selected AND final_carry
lessons.pitfall: Showing a carry from the adder while the mux is selecting XOR.

question.prompt: When should Z be one?

options.text: When all selected output bits are zero
When any one output bit is zero

question.explanation: Z summarizes equality of the complete result to zero.

lessons.title: Test the ALU as a module
paragraphs: For each operation, test zeros, all ones, single-bit patterns and mixed patterns. Addition also needs carry cases such as 15+1 and long propagation cases such as 7+1. Test selection by keeping A and B constant while changing only the operation bits.

Write the ALU’s interface and opcode mapping next to the module. A different CPU may assign different control bits or include shifts and comparison. These are design choices; gate composition and test discipline are the reusable fundamentals. This lab has no subtraction mode, but the preceding course explains how to add one.
lessons.example:
For A=3,B=5,CIN=0:
AND=1; OR=7; XOR=6; ADD=8
lessons.pitfall: Reusing an opcode mapping from another design without checking it.

question.prompt: Why change only the operation bits during one test?
question.explanation: Fixed operands make a wrong operation mapping easier to detect.

steps: Start with A=3, B=5 and OP1 OP0=11; verify Y=8, Z=0, C=0.
Keep operands fixed and select 00,01,10; expect 1,7,6.
For ADD, set A=15,B=1; verify Y=0,Z=1,C=1.
Choose XOR with equal operands and check Z=1,C=0.
courses.expected: At the preset, Y3…Y0=1000, Z=0 and C=0. Other operation settings produce 1,7 and 6.

bridge.principle: An ALU combines reusable function modules behind a controlled interface.
bridge.minecraft: Build and verify logic and addition modules separately, then add a result selector. Keep the operation controls labelled and allow all candidate paths to settle before capturing Y.
bridge.other: The same partition appears in CPUs built from ICs or FPGA gates, although real architectures may use different operations and optimized circuits.

challenge.task: Extend the ALU plan with subtraction and a documented flag convention.
acceptance: Show operand inversion and carry-in for subtraction.
Give expected values for equal operands, borrow and signed overflow cases.

questions.prompt: Which lab control selects XOR?
questions.explanation: The documented table assigns XOR to binary ten.

questions.prompt: What is 3 AND 5 in four bits?
questions.explanation: 0011 AND 0101 leaves 0001.

questions.prompt: What flag values accompany ADD 15+1?
questions.explanation: The retained result is zero with a final carry.

questions.prompt: Should the lab’s XOR operation expose the unused adder carry?

options.text: No; carry is gated by selection

questions.explanation: Status must match the selected operation.

questions.prompt: Which part turns an instruction into ALU selection bits?
questions.explanation: The ALU implements functions; control chooses which one is needed.

courses.title: 9. Feedback and one-bit memory
courses.summary: Move from combinational circuits to stored state with a NOR latch, including its forbidden input combination.

lessons.title: Why feedback changes the problem
paragraphs: Combinational outputs depend only on current inputs. Memory must distinguish two histories even when the current inputs match. Feeding an output back through a carefully designed circuit creates stable states that can retain information.

Two cross-coupled NOR gates form an active-high SR latch. S requests set and R requests reset. Its feedback is intentional; an arbitrary loop of inverters may instead oscillate or be physically unstable. The ordinary gate editor rejects combinational loops, so this lesson uses a dedicated settled-state latch model.
lessons.example:
Q = NOT(R OR Qbar)
Qbar = NOT(S OR Q)
lessons.pitfall: Assuming any loop of gates is a useful memory cell.

question.prompt: What makes a latch different from a combinational gate?

options.text: Its output can depend on earlier inputs

question.explanation: Memory distinguishes histories.

lessons.title: Set, reset and hold
paragraphs: With S=1,R=0, the latch settles to Q=1 and Qbar=0. With S=0,R=1 it settles to Q=0 and Qbar=1. With both inputs zero, feedback holds the previous valid state.

Test hold after both a set and a reset. Seeing Q=0 with S=R=0 does not prove that hold works, because a circuit stuck at zero produces that result too. A useful memory test deliberately creates both histories.
lessons.example:
S R | action
1 0 | set
0 1 | reset
0 0 | hold
lessons.pitfall: Testing hold only after the initial zero state.

question.prompt: After set is released to S=R=0, what should Q do?
question.explanation: Valid feedback retains the set state.

lessons.title: The forbidden combination
paragraphs: For a cross-coupled NOR latch, S=R=1 forces both physical outputs low. They no longer represent a complementary Q/Qbar pair. Releasing both simultaneously does not provide a dependable choice of stored bit.

The bench marks the logical state unknown after this condition and keeps it unknown on hold. Apply only set or only reset to recover a known state. This is a conservative teaching rule; no analog metastability or edition-specific redstone update order is simulated.
lessons.example:
S=R=1: physical outputs 0,0; stored bit invalid
Then S=R=0: unknown until a valid set/reset
lessons.pitfall: Calling the forbidden input a useful toggle operation.

question.prompt: How do you recover a known state after the forbidden combination?

options.text: Apply set alone or reset alone

question.explanation: A valid one-sided request establishes a known stable state.

lessons.title: Latches, enables and clocks
paragraphs: An SR latch reacts to set/reset levels. A gated D latch can derive S=EN AND D and R=EN AND NOT D; while enabled it follows D, and while disabled it holds. An edge-triggered D flip-flop has a different contract: it samples at an edge.

You can build edge-triggered storage from appropriately controlled latch stages, but real clock inversion and propagation require timing care. Learn the interface first. Do not describe a transparent latch as a register that updates exactly once merely because its enable is called clock.
lessons.example:
D latch: transparent while enabled
D flip-flop: samples at a specified edge
lessons.pitfall: Equating a level-sensitive enable with an edge-triggered clock.

question.prompt: What does a transparent D latch do while enabled?
question.explanation: A level-sensitive latch remains open during the enable interval.

steps: Set S=1,R=0 and apply the latch inputs; Q becomes 1.
Set S=R=0 and apply again; Q must remain 1.
Try S=R=1, then release both; inspect the unknown logical state.
Apply reset alone, then release it and verify a stable zero.
courses.expected: The model begins at known zero. Set then hold retains one; forbidden inputs then hold remain unknown until a valid set/reset.

bridge.principle: State requires a specified update rule and a defined initialization procedure.
bridge.minecraft: Use a verified latch design for your Minecraft edition. Test both hold histories and define a reset action instead of relying on block update order at startup.
bridge.other: Relay feedback or electronic latches can retain a bit, but their timing and invalid-state recovery need physical verification.

challenge.task: Write a latch test sequence that catches a device stuck at zero or one.
acceptance: Include set→hold and reset→hold.
Document forbidden input handling and recovery.

questions.prompt: What does S=0,R=1 request on this NOR latch?
questions.explanation: The active-high R input forces Q to zero.

questions.prompt: After reset then hold, what is Q?
questions.explanation: Hold preserves the last valid zero.

questions.prompt: What are the physical NOR outputs while S=R=1?
questions.explanation: Each NOR has a high external input, forcing its output low.

questions.prompt: Does the bench prove a physical latch cannot become metastable?

options.text: No; it models only settled logical behavior

questions.explanation: Physical transient behavior is outside the model.

questions.prompt: Which storage element samples only at an edge?
questions.explanation: The edge-triggered contract separates sampling from the rest of the clock cycle.

courses.title: 10. Flip-flops, registers and clock edges
courses.summary: Store four bits together, control writes, and learn why every register must sample the old state on the same edge.

lessons.title: One flip-flop per stored bit
paragraphs: A D flip-flop stores one bit. A four-bit register uses four copies with a common clock. The data inputs can change while the stored Q outputs remain unchanged; the next active edge captures the selected data.

The lab models a rising edge through the Clock one edge button. There is no continuously running clock or physical clock waveform. All Q values start at zero so experiments are repeatable, whereas a real build needs a reset or another initialization procedure.
lessons.example: D[3:0]=0101; before edge Q=0000; after enabled edge Q=0101
lessons.pitfall: Expecting data input edits to immediately change an edge-triggered register.

question.prompt: When does this register capture its data?

options.text: On Clock one edge with EN=1
Whenever the page is opened in another language

question.explanation: The explicit edge is the state-update event.

lessons.title: Enable and synchronous reset
paragraphs: A write enable chooses between new data and the old Q value. Conceptually Dselected=MUX(Q,D,EN). The lab’s DFF syntax is DFF data enable reset. Reset has priority over enable, and it is synchronous: it takes effect only at an edge.

When EN=0, changing D should not alter Q even when you clock. When RST=1, the next edge sets Q to zero regardless of D or EN. The contract names reset polarity and timing so another implementation can match it.
lessons.example:
if RST: Qnext=0
else if EN: Qnext=D
else: Qnext=Q
lessons.pitfall: Calling this synchronous reset asynchronous.

question.prompt: What happens with EN=0,RST=1 at an edge?
question.explanation: Synchronous reset wins over enable.

lessons.title: Simultaneous sampling preserves pipelines
paragraphs: Imagine q0 loads D and q1 loads q0. At a single edge, q1 must receive the old q0, not the newly written value. Every register samples the pre-edge combinational inputs before any stored output is replaced.

Sequentially updating registers in source order would make behavior depend on the order of lines and could move data through several stages in one edge. The engine computes all next-state values first, then commits them together. This is the correct logical abstraction for a synchronous register bank.
lessons.example:
Before: D=1,q0=0,q1=0
Edge 1: q0=1,q1=0
Edge 2: q0=1,q1=1
lessons.pitfall: Updating q1 from the new q0 within the same edge.

question.prompt: In a two-stage shift register, how many edges move new D to q1?
question.explanation: The second register samples the previous first-register value.

lessons.title: Timing is part of the contract
paragraphs: Real data must be stable for a setup interval before the edge and a hold interval after it. Between edges, allow clock-to-Q delay, combinational delay and setup time, with allowance for clock skew. An ideal Boolean result does not establish a safe physical frequency.

For a Minecraft CPU, begin with a manual clock and observe the slowest path. A long wire, repeater or different component can change the required interval. Increase speed only after testing the full data and control paths in the target edition.
lessons.example: clock period ≥ clock-to-Q + longest logic path + setup allowance
lessons.pitfall: Choosing clock speed from the number of data bits alone.

question.prompt: Why can a faster physical clock cause wrong values?

options.text: Data may not settle before sampling

question.explanation: Setup and propagation constraints limit reliable clocking.

steps: Evaluate the four-bit register with D=0101 and EN=1; Q is initially zero.
Clock one edge; Q becomes five. Turn EN off, change D, and clock again; Q must hold five.
Set RST=1 and clock; Q becomes zero.
Edit a two-DFF pipeline and verify that data takes two edges to reach the second register.
courses.expected: The preset stores five on its first enabled edge. Disable holds that value; synchronous reset clears it on an edge.

bridge.principle: Registers separate stable old state from combinational next-state computation.
bridge.minecraft: Give every register bank the same deliberate capture event. Test reset and load/hold with a slow clock before attaching the ALU.
bridge.other: Electronic flip-flops and FPGA registers use the same next-state reasoning, with device-specific setup, hold and clock constraints.

challenge.task: Build a four-bit loadable counter from an adder, mux and register.
acceptance: Specify reset, load, count and hold priority.
Show a two-edge trace demonstrating old-state sampling.

questions.prompt: How many one-bit DFFs hold four data bits?
questions.explanation: One storage bit is required per bit position.

questions.prompt: What does EN=0 do when reset is inactive?
questions.explanation: The enable selects the old state.

questions.prompt: When is synchronous reset applied?
questions.explanation: Its effect follows the same sampling event as data.

questions.prompt: Should changing the order of DFF lines change a synchronous pipeline?

options.text: Yes; later lines get new values

questions.explanation: Logical simultaneous sampling is independent of source order.

questions.prompt: Which verification remains necessary outside this ideal lab?

options.text: Physical setup, hold and propagation timing

questions.explanation: The model has no physical delay or metastability simulation.

courses.title: 11. Addressable memory and stored programs
courses.summary: Combine registers, decoders and muxes into memory, then separate program words from data words.

lessons.title: Address selects a stored word
paragraphs: Memory is a collection of storage locations with an address interface. Two address bits select four locations. Our small gate experiment has four words of one bit each, making every storage cell visible. Capacity is four bits, not four bytes.

A larger word repeats the storage and read selection for each bit position, sharing the address and control. Address width determines the number of locations; word width determines how much information each location holds. These are independent design choices.
lessons.example: 2 address bits × 1-bit words → 4 locations, 4 stored bits
lessons.pitfall: Confusing word count with word width.

question.prompt: How many locations can two address bits select?
question.explanation: The address has four possible patterns.

lessons.title: Decode writes and preserve other words
paragraphs: For each location, AND its address-decoder output with WE. This becomes that word’s register enable. At an edge, only the selected word captures D. When WE=0, all words hold. RST is a separate synchronous reset of the whole bank in this model.

Test isolation by writing a one to one address and reading every other address. Then write a different address and check the first remains unchanged. A memory that always writes every word can pass a read-after-write test at a single address.
lessons.example: enable[i] = WE AND (address == i)
lessons.pitfall: Testing only the address most recently written.

question.prompt: What must happen to unselected locations during a write?
question.explanation: Only the selected word’s write enable is active.

lessons.title: Read selection is a mux tree
paragraphs: Reading this memory selects Q from the addressed word through a mux tree. It is asynchronous in the ideal model: changing the address changes the selected output after combinational evaluation, without writing any cell. Real devices may instead use synchronous reads.

During a write edge, the state changes and the displayed read output is recomputed from the new state. Document this behavior instead of assuming every RAM shares it. Read/write timing and simultaneous-access policies are part of a memory interface.
lessons.example: DATA = MUX(MUX(q0,q1,A0), MUX(q2,q3,A0), A1)
lessons.pitfall: Assuming all RAM chips have this teaching model’s read timing.

question.prompt: Does reading a different address change the stored cells here?

options.text: Yes; the address is stored as data
No; it only changes the selected output

question.explanation: The read mux observes Q without a write edge.

lessons.title: Program memory and data memory
paragraphs: The later VQ4 CPU has separate program ROM with sixteen eight-bit instructions and data RAM with sixteen four-bit words. A four-bit address selects either memory, but instruction and data buses have different widths. STA writes data RAM, never the program ROM.

This separation is often called a Harvard organization. Other machines use a unified address space. Neither choice determines whether gates can be built in redstone. The important questions are which bus accesses which memory and which operations can change it.
lessons.example:
ROM: 16×8 = 128 bits
RAM: 16×4 = 64 bits
lessons.pitfall: Expecting STA to rewrite the next instruction in this CPU.

question.prompt: Where does VQ4 STA write?
question.explanation: The teaching ISA separates writable data from program storage.

steps: Evaluate the preset, then clock to write 1 to address 01.
Turn WE off and inspect all four addresses; only Q1 should contain 1.
Write 1 to address 10; verify Q1 and Q2 are both retained.
Set RST=1 and clock to clear the whole bank.
courses.expected: After the first write, Q1=1 and Q0,Q2,Q3=0. Read selection does not alter any stored bit.

bridge.principle: Memory behavior combines storage, addressing and a write protocol.
bridge.minecraft: Build one memory row first, then add a decoder and read selector. Leave probes on each write enable to catch unintended simultaneous writes.
bridge.other: The same decomposition explains register files and small RAMs, even when commercial memories implement the cells very differently.

challenge.task: Plan a four-word, four-bit RAM by widening this one-bit design.
acceptance: Account for sixteen stored bits, shared address and write controls.
Test isolated writes, retained earlier data and read behavior.

questions.prompt: What is the capacity of four one-bit words?
questions.explanation: There is one stored bit per location.

questions.prompt: What condition enables a particular write?
questions.explanation: Writing requires both selection and permission.

questions.prompt: What does WE=0 guarantee in this model when reset is inactive?

options.text: Every word holds across the edge
The read output is always zero

questions.explanation: No register enable is active.

questions.prompt: How wide is a VQ4 program word?
questions.explanation: It contains a four-bit opcode and four-bit operand.

questions.prompt: Why test other locations after a write?
questions.explanation: Isolation is essential to addressable storage.

courses.title: 12. A CPU is datapath plus control
courses.summary: Follow the program counter, instruction register, accumulator, ALU and memory through a complete instruction cycle.

lessons.title: The datapath moves and transforms bits
paragraphs: The accumulator A holds the current four-bit working value. The ALU transforms it using an immediate operand or RAM value. PC points to a program word, IR holds the fetched eight-bit instruction, and OUT retains the last value sent to the output.

These blocks have different jobs even though each is made from gates and storage. A CPU becomes programmable when instruction bits determine the sequence of data movement and operations. The lab is a functional microstep model, not a transistor-level implementation.
lessons.example:
PC → program ROM → IR → decode
A + selected operand → ALU → A → OUT
lessons.pitfall: Calling an adder alone a programmable CPU.

question.prompt: Which register holds the instruction being executed?
question.explanation: IR is the instruction register.

lessons.title: Fetch captures the next instruction
paragraphs: On a fetch clock, IR receives ROM[PC] and PC increments modulo sixteen. The old PC is used for the memory read. Consequently PC already points to the next instruction while the current instruction is decoded and executed.

For LDI 3 at address zero, the fetched byte is hex 13. IR becomes 0x13 and PC becomes one, while A is unchanged. The trace distinguishes a fetched instruction from its later effects; seeing the byte in IR does not mean LDI has executed.
lessons.example: FETCH: IR ← ROM[PC]; PC ← (PC+1) mod 16
lessons.pitfall: Expecting A to change during fetch.

question.prompt: Immediately after fetching LDI 3 from address zero, what changed?
question.explanation: Fetch reads the word and advances PC; execute writes A later.

lessons.title: Decode chooses a control action
paragraphs: The high four bits of IR choose one of sixteen opcodes. The low four bits are an immediate value or address depending on the opcode. Decode identifies the operation; execute enables the needed destination and ALU function.

This lab uses three explicit phases per instruction: fetch, decode, execute. Real CPUs can combine phases or pipeline many instructions, but those optimizations preserve an architectural behavior. VQ4 makes the phases visible so control can be traced one event at a time.
lessons.example: 0x13 = opcode 1 (LDI), operand 3
lessons.pitfall: Treating every low nibble as a RAM address.

question.prompt: For LDI 3, how is the low nibble interpreted?
question.explanation: LDI loads a literal encoded in the instruction.

lessons.title: Reset and halting are explicit behaviors
paragraphs: Reset creates zeroed RAM and registers, sets PC=0, sets Z=1 because A=0, clears C, and starts in fetch. HLT takes effect on its execute phase. The program ROM stays the assembled program. Empty ROM locations contain HLT for predictable fall-through.

The browser limits a run to 768 total clocks, including manually stepped clocks, so an infinite loop cannot freeze the page. Hitting that bound pauses the experiment; it is not a successful HLT. Editing source clears the old run, and reset begins a new one.
lessons.example:
LDI 3; ADDI 5; OUT; HLT
4 instructions × 3 phases = 12 clocks
lessons.pitfall: Reporting a clock-limit pause as normal program completion.

question.prompt: How many clocks execute the four-instruction preset through HLT?
question.explanation: Each instruction uses fetch, decode and execute.

steps: Assemble the example and inspect its bytes.
Step fetch, decode and execute for LDI 3; A changes only on the third step.
Run to halt and inspect A, OUT and the trace; the output is eight.
Reset, change ADDI 5 to ADDI 2, and verify a newly assembled run outputs five.
courses.expected: The original program halts after twelve clocks with A=8, OUT=8 and output history [8].

bridge.principle: A CPU is a repeatable state transition controlled by stored instructions.
bridge.minecraft: Construct and test PC, IR, A, memory and output modules separately. A manual three-phase controller is easier to inspect than a fast automatic clock.
bridge.other: A different medium or ISA may use different widths and phase counts while keeping the fetch/decode/execute reasoning.

challenge.task: Draw the control schedule for LDI, ADDI, OUT and HLT.
acceptance: Name every register written in each phase.
Record a complete twelve-clock trace and explain PC before and after fetch.

questions.prompt: Which register points to the next program word?
questions.explanation: The program counter supplies the fetch address.

questions.prompt: What is the high nibble of a VQ4 instruction?
questions.explanation: The opcode selects the instruction behavior.

questions.prompt: When does OUT copy A?
questions.explanation: The output register has its own write control.

questions.prompt: What happens when PC increments past fifteen?
questions.explanation: PC is a four-bit register; HLT is a separate instruction.

questions.prompt: What does reaching 768 clocks indicate?

options.text: The bounded run stopped without necessarily halting

questions.explanation: The execution cap is a browser limit, not an instruction.

courses.title: 13. Assembly language and machine code
courses.summary: Read mnemonics, operands and labels, and assemble a program into the exact bits a CPU fetches.

lessons.title: An ISA is a contract
paragraphs: An instruction set architecture specifies instructions and their visible effects. Assembly is a readable notation for that contract. An assembler converts the notation to machine words; the CPU decodes those words, not the English-like instruction names.

This editor runs VQ4, an original teaching ISA with a four-bit accumulator and eight-bit instruction words. It is not x86, ARM, AVR, ESP32 or RISC-V assembly. The skills of tracking registers, operands and branches transfer; encodings and syntax must be relearned for each ISA.
lessons.pitfall: Assuming a mnemonic means the same thing on every CPU.

question.prompt: What does an assembler primarily produce?

options.text: A new instruction set for every source line

question.explanation: It maps source notation to the selected ISA’s binary instructions.

lessons.title: Mnemonics and numeric literals
paragraphs: LDI 10, LDI 0xA and LDI 0b1010 encode the same byte. Decimal, hexadecimal and binary notation affect how the source is written, not how many bits the value occupies. VQ4 operands must fit from zero through fifteen.

Comments begin with a semicolon and consume no program location. Instructions are case-insensitive. NOP, OUT and HLT take no operand; the other instructions take one. The assembler rejects extra operands and unsupported syntax instead of silently changing the meaning.
lessons.example:
LDI 0b1010 ; decimal ten
OUT
HLT
lessons.pitfall: Treating 0x10 as decimal ten; it is decimal sixteen and does not fit an operand.

question.prompt: Which literal fits four bits and equals decimal ten?
question.explanation: Hexadecimal A denotes ten.

lessons.title: Labels name code addresses
paragraphs: A label marks the address of the next instruction. JMP, JZ and JC may use defined labels; the assembler resolves them before execution. Labels and comments do not increase program length. Numeric jumps specify absolute instruction addresses in this ISA.

The sixteen-word ROM makes counting addresses manageable, but labels prevent many mistakes when instructions are inserted. A code label is not automatically a data-memory symbol. VQ4 load/store operands remain numeric RAM addresses so the two spaces are not confused.
lessons.example:
start: LDI 3
JMP start
; start resolves to ROM address 0
lessons.pitfall: Counting a standalone label as an instruction.

question.prompt: Does a label occupy a VQ4 instruction word?

options.text: Only if it has a long name

question.explanation: A label is an assembler name for an address.

lessons.title: Inspect the listing and the executed word
paragraphs: The assembler listing pairs source lines with addresses, binary words and hexadecimal words. Use it to check opcode and operand fields independently. The CPU executes the encoded ROM byte, so the listing is a useful bridge between readable source and actual state changes.

Assemble-time errors include undefined branch labels, duplicate labels, invalid literals and more than sixteen instructions. A syntactically valid program can still be logically wrong. Step it and compare register effects with an expected trace rather than treating successful assembly as proof.
lessons.example:
0xC0 = OUT
0xD0 = HLT
lessons.pitfall: Equating successful assembly with correct program behavior.

question.prompt: What does a successful assembly prove?

options.text: The source fits the supported syntax and encoding rules

question.explanation: Execution and physical implementation require additional checks.

steps: Assemble the preset and compare the three LDI bytes; each must be 0x1A.
Run and verify three outputs of ten.
Change one literal to 0x10 and assemble; read the range error.
Restore a valid literal, add a comment and show that addresses do not change.
courses.expected: The program outputs [10,10,10]. Each numeric spelling of ten produces the same LDI byte.

bridge.principle: Readable instruction names and binary encoding are two views of the same ISA.
bridge.minecraft: Program ROM can be a manually configured bank of bits. Transfer the listing’s bytes in address order, checking every opcode and operand bit.
bridge.other: Real assemblers also handle labels and encodings, but directives, pseudo-instructions, word widths and instruction lengths vary.

challenge.task: Encode LDI 6, OUT, HLT by hand, then compare the listing.
acceptance: Show binary and hexadecimal bytes for all three instructions.
Explain why source comments do not require ROM cells.

questions.prompt: What is VQ4 LDI 6 in hexadecimal?
questions.explanation: Opcode one is the high nibble and six is the low nibble.

questions.prompt: Which is a valid no-operand instruction?
questions.explanation: OUT takes no operand; LDI needs one.

questions.prompt: Where does a label resolve?

options.text: The address of the following instruction

questions.explanation: Labels identify code locations.

questions.prompt: Which source feature changes no program addresses?
questions.explanation: Comments do not emit words.

questions.prompt: Will this editor run an arbitrary RISC-V program?

options.text: Only if every label is lowercase

questions.explanation: ISA encodings and syntax are specific contracts.

courses.title: 14. Registers, immediate values and memory operands
courses.summary: Plan where values live, preserve them with stores, and distinguish a value from its address.

lessons.title: The accumulator is a working register
paragraphs: VQ4 has one general working register, A. LDI replaces it with a literal. If an earlier value is still needed, save it before overwriting A. Register scarcity makes the dataflow visible: instructions cannot remember a value merely because it appeared in an earlier source line.

The preset saves six in RAM[3], loads two, and adds the saved value to make eight. This is an elementary version of managing temporaries on larger processors. Real ISAs often provide several working registers and different operand counts.
lessons.example:
LDI 6
STA 3
LDI 2
ADD 3
lessons.pitfall: Expecting LDI 2 to keep the previous six inside A as well.

question.prompt: How can VQ4 preserve A before replacing it?
question.explanation: STA copies A into an addressed data location.

lessons.title: Immediate and direct addressing
paragraphs: An immediate operand is part of the instruction itself. LDI 3 loads the value three. A direct memory operand names a location: LDA 3 loads whatever is stored at RAM[3]. The same low nibble is interpreted differently according to the opcode.

To diagnose a wrong result, ask whether the instruction needs a value or an address. In the preset RAM[3] is six, so LDA 3 produces six, not three. VQ4 has no indirect addressing, byte pointers or variable-width loads.
lessons.example:
LDI 3 → A=3
LDA 3 → A=RAM[3]
lessons.pitfall: Confusing an address with the value located there.

question.prompt: If RAM[3]=6, what does LDA 3 produce?
question.explanation: LDA reads the addressed data word.

lessons.title: Stores copy data and keep the working value
paragraphs: STA 4 copies A to RAM[4] and leaves A unchanged. It also preserves Z and C in this ISA. A following load can recover an earlier temporary or a completed result. Program ROM is separate, so these writes cannot modify code.

A useful memory map assigns purposes to addresses, such as RAM[3]=saved input and RAM[4]=sum. Write that map before the program, avoid accidental overlap, and test that unrelated locations remain unchanged. Larger systems use allocation and calling conventions for the same reason.
lessons.example:
RAM[3]: original value 6
RAM[4]: result 8
lessons.pitfall: Using one address for two values whose lifetimes overlap.

question.prompt: After STA 4, what happens to A?
question.explanation: Store copies A without consuming it.

lessons.title: Output is another retained register
paragraphs: OUT copies A to the output register and appends that value to the observable history. Later changes to A do not change OUT until another OUT executes. This lets a display hold a result while the CPU continues computing.

Trace both internal state and external output. The preset prints the preserved six, then the computed eight. A final A=8 alone would not prove the earlier six was preserved and output correctly. Observations should match the whole intended sequence.
lessons.example: Expected output sequence: 6, 8
lessons.pitfall: Checking only the final accumulator when the requirement includes several outputs.

question.prompt: After OUT then LDI 2, what remains in OUT?
question.explanation: OUT has its own stored state.

steps: Assemble and step through the first store; inspect RAM[3]=6.
Run the preset to halt; inspect RAM[4]=8 and output history [6,8].
Change LDA 3 near the end to LDI 3 and observe the first output become three.
Restore it and explain every operand as either a literal or a RAM address.
courses.expected: The original program preserves RAM[3]=6, stores RAM[4]=8 and outputs [6,8].

bridge.principle: A memory map and register trace make value lifetimes explicit.
bridge.minecraft: Use a small labelled RAM bank for temporaries and a separate output latch driving lamps. Verify a store does not disturb the selected program word.
bridge.other: On a register-rich ISA, temporary values may stay in registers; spills and loads follow the same preserve-before-overwrite reasoning.

challenge.task: Write a program that saves two inputs, adds them and outputs both the original first input and the sum.
acceptance: Document each RAM address’s purpose.
Check that stores leave the accumulator intact and output changes only at OUT.

questions.prompt: Which instruction loads the literal seven?
questions.explanation: LDI selects an immediate value.

questions.prompt: What does ADD 3 use as its second operand?
questions.explanation: ADD is direct-memory addition; ADDI adds a literal.

questions.prompt: Which memory can STA change?
questions.explanation: The VQ4 memory spaces are separate.

questions.prompt: Why assign temporary values different addresses when both are still needed?

options.text: To make labels take more space
To avoid overwriting a live value

questions.explanation: Memory locations hold one current value each.

questions.prompt: What observation proves the preset preserved six and then produced eight?
questions.explanation: The sequence demonstrates both the preserved input and later result.

courses.title: 15. Arithmetic, bit masks and status flags
courses.summary: Use wraparound and status flags deliberately, and branch before another instruction replaces the evidence.

lessons.title: Arithmetic has a width
paragraphs: ADDI adds a literal; ADD reads a RAM operand. Both keep the low four bits in A and set C from the carry. SUBI and SUB use two’s-complement addition and set C=1 when no unsigned borrow is needed.

VQ4 Z describes whether the new A is zero. LDI and LDA also update Z and clear C; AND, OR and XOR do the same. STA, jumps, OUT, NOP and HLT preserve both flags. A flag is stored state with a defined writer, not a permanent description of an earlier calculation.
lessons.example: LDI 15; ADDI 1 → A=0, Z=1, C=1
lessons.pitfall: Assuming flags survive a later load.

question.prompt: After LDI 15 then ADDI 1, what are A,Z,C?
question.explanation: The four-bit result wraps to zero with a carry.

lessons.title: Use flags while they are relevant
paragraphs: JC branches when C=1 and JZ branches when Z=1. A branch does not change A or flags. In the preset, JC directly follows the addition so it observes that addition’s carry.

Inserting LDI between ADDI and JC clears C and changes the branch decision. This is a data dependency even though no explicit register operand appears in the branch source. Annotate flag lifetimes just as you annotate temporary-value lifetimes.
lessons.example:
ADDI 1
JC carry
; a flag-writing instruction here would matter
lessons.pitfall: Reading a stale flag after another instruction has updated it.

question.prompt: Why must a carry test consider intervening instructions?
question.explanation: Flag-writing instructions replace the condition being tested.

lessons.title: Masks select or change bit positions
paragraphs: AND with a mask clears positions where the mask is zero. OR sets positions where the mask is one. XOR toggles those positions. In VQ4 the mask is first stored in RAM because these logical instructions use memory operands.

For A=1010 and mask=0011, AND gives 0010, OR gives 1011 and XOR gives 1001. These are per-bit transformations. They are useful for lamp panels, packed status bits and extracting fields even when the bus is not interpreted as a number.
lessons.pitfall: Expecting AND to add the mask or to return only a whole-word Boolean.

question.prompt: Which operation toggles bits selected by a mask?
question.explanation: XOR with one reverses a bit and XOR with zero preserves it.

lessons.title: Signed meaning needs separate reasoning
paragraphs: VQ4 has no signed-overflow flag and no signed comparison instruction. Its carry branches are useful for unsigned arithmetic under the documented convention. Four-bit 1000 may mean unsigned eight or signed minus eight; the flag alone does not choose an interpretation.

For 0−1, A=15, Z=0 and C=0. For 5−3, A=2 and C=1. Compare these examples with a real ISA manual before porting: flag conventions differ, and RISC-V base integer branches do not use a global condition-code register.
lessons.example: SUBI 1 after A=0 → A=15, C=0 (borrow)
lessons.pitfall: Porting a carry branch without checking the target ISA’s subtraction convention.

question.prompt: What does VQ4 C=0 indicate after 0−1?
question.explanation: The subtraction construction has no final carry when a borrow is needed.

steps: Run the preset: addition wraps to zero, JC takes the carry branch, and OUT emits zero.
Continue through SUBI 1 and OUT; the second output is fifteen with C=0.
Insert LDI 2 before JC; observe that it clears C and changes control flow.
Restore the source and use stepping to identify every flag-writing instruction.
courses.expected: The original program outputs [0,15]. The carry branch is taken after 15+1; subtracting one from zero clears C.

bridge.principle: Status flags are explicit dependencies with instruction-specific lifetimes.
bridge.minecraft: Expose Z and C on lamps beside the accumulator. Capture them with the arithmetic result and keep the branch decoder connected to the stored flags.
bridge.other: Check target ISA manuals for flag behavior. Some ISAs compare registers directly instead of branching on stored flags.

challenge.task: Write a program that detects unsigned wraparound and outputs a different marker for carry and no carry.
acceptance: Test 15+1 and 3+1.
Ensure no instruction overwrites flags before the branch.

questions.prompt: What does ADDI use?
questions.explanation: ADDI adds the low-nibble literal.

questions.prompt: Which instruction preserves C in VQ4?
questions.explanation: Store preserves flags; loads and logic update them.

questions.prompt: What is 1010 OR 0011?
questions.explanation: OR sets any position present in either operand.

questions.prompt: Does VQ4 C directly represent signed overflow?
questions.explanation: Carry and signed overflow are different conditions.

questions.prompt: For A=5 then SUBI 3, what are A and C?
questions.explanation: No unsigned borrow is required.
